parts:
library(blavaan)
df.IJS5=readRDS("df.SIJS5.rds")

IJS5 <- '
JobSatisfaction =~ IJS.JIS1. + IJS.JIS2. + IJS.JIS3. + IJS.JIS4. + IJS.JIS5.
'

## fit target model
fit1 <- bcfa(IJS5, data = df.IJS5, cp = "srs",
             n.chains = 2, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000)


## fit null model to calculate CFI, TLI, and NFI
null.model <- c(paste0("IJS.JIS", 1:5,".", " ~~ IJS.JIS", 1:5,"."), paste0("IJS.JIS", 1:5,"."," ~ 1"))
fit0 <- bcfa(null.model, data = df.IJS5, cp = "srs",
             n.chains = 2, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000)


## calculate posterior distributions of fit indices


## The default method mimics fit indices derived from ML estimation
ML <- blavFitIndices(fit1, baseline.model = fit0)
ML
summary(ML)

The result of the `fitMeasures` is:


> fitMeasures(fit1)

     looic      p_loo     se_loo margloglik
 16020.605     21.717    179.673  -8070.463

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Calculate posterior distributions of fit indices (NaN BRMSEA value)
parts:
Jorge

This happened because of the curious behavior of the pD (effective number of parameters). You are using default priors, so the bayesian effective number of parameters should be really close to the frequentist number of parameters (npar). In the simulation testing the fit indices, the LOO and WAIC based pD performed better and closer to the expected behavior.

For reasons I cannot understand without the data set, you LOO and WAIC pDs are higher (~ 20) than the frequentist 15. So this is causing a problem with the calculations as turns the "degrees of freedom" into negative. Weirdly enough the DIC pD is close to the expected npar.

So,
- First: check that your model has converged. Meaning the PSRF is lower than 1.05 for every parameter blavInspect(fit1, "psrf"). If not, run the model for longer burnin, and check the pDs
- Second: If this bechavior of the pDs is there whit a converged model, change to use the DIC based pD for the fit indices calculations ML <- blavFitIndices(fit1, baseline.model = fit0, pD="dic")


Hope this helps

Glad that worked.

I dont know what could lead to this behavior, would have to check in more detail the data set.

This means that DIC is agreeing with npar about the estimated information, while LOO is saying that more information is estimated. Also, this would be less of an issue with bigger models, which woulkd lead to less likely situations with negative "degrees of freedom"

parts:
It may not solve your problem with LOO, but I'd recommend sampling for
more than 1000 iterations. It can take a large number of samples to
get DIC/WAIC/etc to converge to a stable value.

Ed
